questions.text: Which of the following is the most appropriate title for the passage?
questions.context: Asked to predict how a stranger will react to a minor inconvenience — a delayed flight, a spilled coffee, a rude comment — most people forecast a stronger and longer-lasting emotional reaction than the stranger actually reports experiencing once the event occurs. The same overestimation applies to our own future feelings: people preparing for a breakup, a job loss, or a disappointing exam result consistently predict deeper and more prolonged misery than they later recall actually feeling. Human beings, it turns out, are reliably poor forecasters of their own emotional resilience, routinely underestimating how quickly both good and bad feelings fade.

options.text: Why Strangers Misjudge Each Other's Emotions
The Durability Bias: Why We Overestimate How Long Feelings Last
How to Accurately Predict a Stranger's Reaction
The Emotional Cost of Job Loss and Exam Failure
Why Coffee Spills Provoke Stronger Reactions Than Expected

questions.text: Choose the most appropriate topic of the passage.
questions.context: Quite often the interaction between two people negotiating is not a pure conflict but a mix of shared and opposing interests, and the strategies suited to one differ sharply from strategies suited to the other. Treating a negotiation with substantial shared interest — dividing a shared resource both parties want preserved, say — as if it were purely adversarial tends to leave value unclaimed on the table, since neither side explores the trades that would have benefited both. Conversely, treating a purely adversarial negotiation as if goodwill alone will produce a fair split often leaves one side badly exploited.

options.text: why negotiations always contain more shared interest than conflict
how mismatching a negotiation strategy to its actual mix of shared and opposing interests carries real costs
techniques for dividing shared resources fairly between two parties
the psychological profile of a successful negotiator
why adversarial negotiations are more common than cooperative ones

questions.text: Choose the most appropriate topic of the passage.
questions.context: Cities founded along a navigable river or a natural harbour often retain their commercial advantage for centuries after the original reason for the advantage has become irrelevant to modern transport, a pattern economists call path dependence. Rail lines were built to connect to already-established ports; roads and later motorways were built to connect to already-established rail hubs; each new layer of infrastructure reinforced advantages that were, by the time of construction, no longer tied to any river or harbour at all. Undoing this accumulated advantage would require abandoning enormous sunk infrastructure investments, which is why geographically arbitrary historical accidents can shape a country's economic geography for centuries.

options.text: the engineering techniques used to build early rail networks
how early geographic advantages become self-reinforcing through successive infrastructure investment
why rivers and harbours are no longer relevant to modern transport
the total economic output of port cities compared to inland cities
methods for relocating infrastructure away from historically advantaged regions

questions.text: Which of the following best states the main point of the passage?
questions.context: A committee tasked with approving a project rarely does so through a single, decisive vote; instead, the project accumulates small procedural approvals — a budget line here, a preliminary sign-off there — each of which feels individually minor and reversible, until the accumulated momentum makes cancelling the project feel far more costly than continuing it, regardless of whether continuing is actually the better choice. No single approval was ever a considered commitment to the whole; the commitment emerged from the sum of steps that each felt too small to refuse.

options.text: Committees should require a single, decisive vote before approving any major project.
Large commitments can accumulate gradually through small approvals that individually feel minor and reversible.
Procedural approvals are always a more considered decision than a single decisive vote.
Projects are cancelled more often than they are approved once procedural momentum builds.
Committees are generally more rational than individual decision-makers.

questions.text: How many of the statements below do NOT agree with the passage?
questions.context:
When I first started coaching my daughter's recreational football team, I ran every drill exactly as I remembered them from my own childhood training, certain that whatever had worked on me would work on eight-year-olds thirty years later. The kids were bored within ten minutes and I blamed their attention spans rather than my drills. A more experienced coach watching from the sideline suggested cutting every drill to a third of its length and adding a competitive element, however small. I resisted at first, assuming this was a concession to laziness rather than a genuine improvement. The shorter, gamified version of the same drills produced noticeably sharper focus almost immediately, and I still feel a flash of embarrassment recalling how long I blamed the children before considering my own methods.

Statements
(a) The writer initially attributed the children's boredom to her coaching methods rather than their attention spans.
(b) A more experienced coach suggested shortening the drills and adding a competitive element.
(c) The writer immediately agreed that the suggested changes were a genuine improvement.
(d) The shortened, gamified drills produced noticeably sharper focus.
(e) The writer still feels some embarrassment about how long she blamed the children.
(f) The writer's original drills were based on her own childhood training.

questions.text: Which statement does NOT agree with the two explanations given in the passage?
questions.context: Firms operating in the same industry often cluster geographically rather than spreading evenly across a country, even when transport costs would seem to favour dispersal. One explanation holds that clustering allows firms to draw on a shared, specialised local labour pool: workers with industry-specific skills move to where the jobs are concentrated, and firms in turn locate where such workers already live, each reinforcing the other. A second, competing explanation emphasises knowledge spillovers: informal contact among employees of nearby competing firms, through shared suppliers, industry events, or simple proximity, spreads innovations faster than could occur if firms were geographically dispersed, giving clustered firms a collective advantage over isolated ones.

options.text: The first explanation attributes clustering to a mutually reinforcing relationship between skilled workers and firms.
The first explanation suggests worker mobility follows the location of specialised job opportunities.
The second explanation attributes clustering to faster informal spread of innovation among nearby firms.
The second explanation agrees with the first that clustering's primary advantage is a shared specialised labour pool.
Both explanations attempt to account for the same observed pattern of industry clustering.

questions.context: Ask someone to wear a slightly embarrassing item into a room of strangers and then estimate what percentage of people noticed it; the guess reliably runs two or three times higher than the number who actually did, according to those same strangers questioned afterward. Underlying this is what researchers call _the spotlight effect_: an assumption that one's own appearance and mistakes occupy far more space in others' attention than they actually do, largely because each of us is so absorbed in our own experience that we mistake that absorption for everyone else's.

options.text: a tendency to deliberately draw attention to one's own mistakes in public

questions.context: Deep-diving sperm whales rely on echolocation to hunt squid in total darkness, producing a rapid series of clicks whose echoes reveal the location, distance, and even approximate size of potential prey hundreds of metres below the surface where no light penetrates at all. Just before striking, a hunting whale emits a distinctive burst of rapid clicks known as a "creak," so tightly spaced they resemble a creaking door, allowing it to update its target's position almost continuously as the final approach closes in. Researchers studying tagged whales have found individual whales develop slightly distinct clicking patterns, suggesting something like individual acoustic signatures.

questions.text: Among the dictionary definitions below, how many describe words that do NOT appear in the passage? (Ignore singular/plural forms, voice, and tense.)
questions.context:
Peer review is meant to filter weak research before publication, but reviewers themselves operate under incentives that can quietly distort the process. A reviewer who recommends rejection risks little, since a rejected paper's fate is invisible to the wider field, while a reviewer who champions a paper that later proves flawed risks visible professional embarrassment. This asymmetry may push reviewers toward excessive caution, rejecting borderline but potentially valuable work rather than risk being publicly associated with an eventual failure. Some journals have experimented with open review, in which reviewer identities and comments are published alongside the paper, specifically to make this asymmetry visible and, proponents hope, correct for it.

Definitions
(a) a lack of balance or equal treatment between two things
(b) to publicly support or advocate strongly for something
(c) careful avoidance of risk or unnecessary danger
(d) a feeling of shame or awkwardness caused by an embarrassing situation
(e) to formally reject or refuse to accept something
(f) able to be perceived or noticed, not hidden
(g) to postpone a decision until further evidence is available
(h) a general tendency to favour one outcome over another

questions.text: Choose the most appropriate place for the given sentence: "Crucially, none of the participants could say why they preferred the repeatedly viewed image over the new one."
questions.context: In one study, participants were briefly shown a series of abstract shapes, some repeated several times across the session, others displayed only once. ( ① ) Afterward, asked simply to rate how much they liked each shape, participants consistently favoured the frequently shown ones over those seen only once. ( ③ ) Researchers call this the mere-exposure effect, and note that it operates below conscious awareness rather than through any deliberate reasoning about familiarity. ( ③ ) An experienced player's bluff, by contrast, is calibrated specifically against what other experienced players expect, making it considerably harder for another expert to distinguish from a genuine strong hand. ( ④ ) Deception, in this sense, is a skill that must be calibrated against a specific, well-informed audience to be effective. ( ⑤ )
